brief.lede: At the Moon's south pole the Sun and Earth stay only a few degrees above the horizon. Whether a point gets sunlight and sees Earth is decided by the real terrain horizon. The numbers here come from that horizon, computed from NASA LOLA elevation data.
brief.period: 2026–2028 · hourly · panel and antenna 2 m above ground · each card shows one point's own numbers (the candidate named on its lower line) · thin strips: that region's candidate 1 in 2027, Sun (top) and Earth with 1° margin (bottom)

sortNote.power: Sorted by the solar energy fraction (time-averaged visible fraction of the disc) of each region's candidate 1. "Sunlit time" on the card is the share of time any part of the disc is visible.
sortNote.comm: Sorted by the share of time Earth is at least 1° above the horizon at each region's candidate 1 (1° antenna margin).
sortNote.dark: Sorted by the longest spell with no Sun at each region's candidate 1.
sortNote.balanced: Score = (a·solar energy % + b·Earth % + c·dark score) / (a + b + c). Dark score = 100 − longest dark / 30 days × 100 (30 days or more scores 0). The card shows the region's best-scoring point for these weights.

data.title: Data and sources
data.status: All numbers are preliminary. This data package has no summary of the comparison with NASA's maps (years.json).
data.statusVal: The numbers are preliminary. The method was compared with NASA's 18.6-year average visibility maps ({period}, {n} random points, 84° S–90° S). Under the maps' conditions (0 m observer on the surface, any part of the disc) the mean absolute difference is {sun} points for the Sun (max {sunMax}) and {earth} points for Earth (max {earthMax}). The numbers in the app are for a 2 m observer; under that condition the difference is {sun2} for the Sun and {earth2} for Earth. No correction was applied. Details: docs/dogrulama.md.
method: For every point a 360° horizon profile (0.25° step) was computed from NASA's LOLA south pole elevation map (80 m/pixel, out to 300 km), including the Moon's curvature.

Sun and Earth positions come from NASA/JPL SPICE, hourly. "Sunlit time" is the share of time any part of the solar disc is visible. "Solar energy fraction" is the mean visible fraction of the disc: half the disc above the horizon counts as 50% power.

Card numbers on the briefing screen cover 2026–2028. Every number in the cockpit (summary, communication, flat-horizon comparison) is a live calculation for the selected year, done in the browser; the comparison screen computes the window after landing. Two periods are never shown side by side in one panel.

Earth visibility is computed for the centre of the disc: the link counts as up when Earth's centre is above the terrain horizon by the antenna margin. A partly visible Earth disc (radius ≈ 0.95°) does not count as a link.
The flat-horizon comparison uses the same Sun/Earth geometry and only sets the horizon to 0°.

Battery under uncertainty: load and panel power are taken as independent and uniformly distributed within the chosen ± range, and tried 1000 times. The probability is the share of trials in which a vehicle landing with a full battery on the selected day survives to the end of the data. The distribution is an assumption.
cand: Screening: inside each region polygon an 800 m grid was laid (at most ~1000 points in large regions) and points with slope under 8° (on the 80 m data) were kept. For each point our model computed 2027 solar energy and Earth visibility; the screening score is their mean. The 20 best points at least 1 km apart became candidates.

Detail: the 20 candidates were recomputed with our model (2 m, 2026–2028) and ranked by balanced score; the candidate number is that rank. The top 5 candidates and the sample point have a full landing package; the others show summary numbers only.
Each card shows the numbers of one point: the region's candidate 1, or, in the Balanced sort, the best-scoring point for the chosen weights.

Landing error: for every point with a landing package the same calculation was repeated in eight directions at 100 m and 300 m from the target. Shown are the worst three numbers among the ring points with slope under 8° (landable) and how many directions exceed an 8° slope. 100 m is an assumption, not a verified NASA requirement. "Zoom to point" shows the rings on the map; a cross marks a direction over the slope limit.
Pareto mark: among the region's 21 points, those for which no other point is better in all three measures. Weights can be changed in the Balanced sort; with equal weights the score is unchanged.
The heat map is NASA's Sun map, not our calculation: share of time any part of the disc is visible, averaged over about 18.6 years for an observer on the surface.
The NASA map used here has 120 m resolution from 75° S to the pole (AVGVISIB_75S_120M_201608).
gloss: Antenna margin (antenna mask): how far above the horizon the antenna needs Earth to be. A 1° margin means the link counts as up only while Earth's centre is at least 1° above the terrain horizon. 0° is the most optimistic assumption.
Critical margin: how little room is left above the horizon while Earth is visible. With a small margin, a small error in the terrain data can turn "visible" into "not visible".

Sunlit time vs solar energy fraction: the first is the share of time any part of the Sun is visible; the second is the mean visible fraction of the disc and is proportional to panel power. While the Sun grazes the horizon the first is larger.
Joint window (Sun + Earth): time when the Sun is visible and the Earth link is up together, i.e. time with both power and a data path.
Pareto point: a point for which no other point in the region is better in all three measures (Sun, Earth, longest dark).
Flat horizon: the simple assumption that there is no terrain and the horizon is 0° in every direction. It is here to show the difference real terrain makes.
limits: Sample point: the screening point nearest the region centre with slope under 8°. Neither the sample point nor the candidates are official landing sites.
Region outlines were digitised from NASA's 28 October 2024 announcement image (about ±1 km); they are not USGS's official polygons.

Candidates were screened only by slope and our illumination/communication model. Rocks, small craters, landing ellipse and temperature are not considered. Terrain is at 80 m resolution; smaller obstacles do not appear in the horizon.
Battery capacity, panel power and load are example values, not data of a real vehicle.
Earth's cloud and land pattern in the 3D scene is illustrative. The lander model is symbolic.
3D shadows only know the 20×20 km terrain tile. Whether the point is lit always comes from the computed data.
The lander's shadow on the ground is illustrative; terrain shadows are computed from real elevation data.
Only points with a full data package (the sample point and the top 5 candidates per region, 54 points) have hourly series; only those can be compared or opened in the cockpit.
For observer heights other than 2 m, the visible fraction of the Sun is recomputed in the browser from the same hourly positions with a constant solar radius of 0.267°.
The 3D scene always draws the 2 m observer's horizon profile; the observer-height choice changes the numbers, the sky radar, the panorama and the strips.
sources: Elevation: NASA LRO/LOLA, Barker et al. 2023, PSJ 4:183, NASA PGDA product 90.
Regions: NASA, 28 October 2024 Artemis III announcement (digitised from the image); official polygons: McClernan 2024, USGS, doi:10.5066/P1MEQ6UK.
Heat map and validation: NASA PGDA product 69, LOLA average Sun and Earth visibility maps (AVGVISIB_75S_120M_201608), Mazarico et al. 2011.
Sun and Earth: NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE, DE440 (de440s.bsp) and lunar orientation (moon_pa_de440_200625.bpc), in the same frame as LOLA, MOON_ME_DE440_ME421.
Inspiration: NASA SVS 5228, Lunar South Pole Illumination with Earth and Sun.

tour.s1: {name}. Terrain from NASA LOLA data, to scale. The Sun stays only a few degrees above the horizon; shadows sweep across the ground.
tour.s2: Astronaut view. The Sun does not rise, it grazes the horizon. The panel gets as much power as the visible part of the disc.
tour.s3: Earth does not set, it sways in place; the faint trace is its path over the data. With this antenna mask there is a link {earth} of the time this year.
tour.s4dead: Longest dark {dark}. An example {cap} kWh battery runs out on mission day {n}.
tour.s4alive: Longest dark {dark}. An example {cap} kWh battery survives to the end of the data with these settings.
tour.s5: A flat-horizon calculation finds {flat} sunlit time for {y}. With the real terrain horizon it is {real}.
tour.s6: The real horizon makes the difference. Numbers are preliminary; see Data and sources for the comparison with NASA's maps.

cmp.how: "Add to comparison" on the briefing or in the cockpit pins the current point, date and antenna margin. For another date at the same point use "Copy − / +" in a column.

cmp.sumTie: The scenarios are level in the joint Sun + Earth window ({v}).

cmp.sumDarkShorter: Its longest dark is {v} days shorter.

rowTitle.sun: Share of the window in which any part of the solar disc is above the terrain horizon.
rowTitle.earth: Share of the window in which Earth's centre is above the terrain horizon by the antenna margin.
rowTitle.both: Share of the window in which the Sun is visible and the Earth link is up together (joint window).
rowTitle.dark: Longest unbroken spell in the window with no part of the Sun visible.
rowTitle.gap: Longest unbroken spell in the window without an Earth link.

cmp.clipped: The window is cut at the end of the data ({end}): only {got} of {want} days were computed.
cmp.landEarth: Earth {rel} the terrain horizon · with {m}° margin: {s}
cmp.noChange: no change to the end of the data
cmp.stripAlt: Scenario {k}: Sun, Earth and joint visibility strips aligned to landing
cmp.copyOut: That date is outside the data.
cmp.openTitle: Click: open this scenario in the cockpit
cmp.readHint: Hover over the strip: date, time and the state at that moment
cmp.foot: The window is aligned to landing; 30 days is about one lunar day (29.5 days). Strips: Sun (visible fraction of the disc), Earth (link), both together. Scenario = point + landing date + antenna margin; battery settings are not part of it. Observer {h} m. A green number is the best in its row; the small number is the difference to A (percentage points for percentages).
